chapter_theme: Kemasari's concealed love is announced by her father, the marriage is held, and two months of bliss likened to the state beyond birth and death follow; then, on a night framed by a sunset told as a life's ageing, Civakan slips away while she sleeps, and she wakes to search for him like a serpent that has lost its gem.

cast.role: the hero, called காளை, மைந்தன், குருசில் and மார்பன் here; married to Kemasari and leaves her in secret
the merchant's daughter of the Takka land whom Civakan marries and leaves (not named in these verses)
Kemasari's father, the merchant, who announces the match to the king
Kemasari's kin and the townspeople who perform the wedding
the parrots of the millet slope
the bee at Kemasari's garland whom Civakan addresses

1485.reading: Keeping her love shut inside her eyes, she makes the eye her messenger to tell him what she has resolved, and hides it so well that her kin find no fault; such a sword-eyed glance would outsell the sea's nectar and the whole world.
1485.nuance: The verse turns on கரந்திட்ட: her love is real but concealed, and the concealment is itself praised because it spares her kin any blame (ஏதின்மை). It may be Civakan's thought rather than the narrator's; the speech of 1487 makes the point uncertain.

1486.reading: Her breasts are figured as war-elephants: crowned with pearls, their fury cooled, decked with bright gems and given a face-cloth of fine gold, beside the garland of massed jasmine.
1486.nuance: The elephant figure (முகபடாம், கடாம்) makes the beloved's body an armed force against the man who sees her, preparing Civakan's complaint in 1487 that her features are Death and Yama's noose.

1487.reading: Civakan says her hair has learned to feed on honey, her spear-eye on flesh, her curved brow is Death and her breasts are Yama's noose, and yet he, a pitiable stranger, sits longing to live.
1487.nuance: The list of killers (கூற்றம், நமன்கைப் பாசம்) ends in the wish to live (வாழ்வான் ஆசைப்பட்டு): the lover desires the very thing he names as death. பிறன் marks him as an outsider in the Takka land.

1488.reading: He tells the golden flower-creeper, a lamp to the beauty of goddesses wearing kalpaka garlands, that one woman's loveliness has made her an enemy to Murugan, to Kama, to himself and to the god of dense matted hair.
1488.nuance: Setting himself beside Murugan, Anangan and the ascetic god of matted locks (மொய்சடை ஒருவன்) makes her beauty a rival even to the god who renounced and burned desire; how பகைத்தி is to be taken, as rivalry or as hostility, is not certain.

1489.reading: While the youth who had passed beyond the many arts brooded on her beauty, the merchant told the king of the land, lord of musth elephants, by due custom, so that the people of the land should know.
1489.event: Kemasari's father, the merchant, formally announces the match to the king and the land.
1489.nuance: The marriage moves at once from the glance of 1485 to a public act: the father's report to the king (நெறியிற் செப்பினான்) is what turns concealed love into an approved union.

1490.reading: With the many instruments of the flag-decked city roaring like the thunder-spitting surf, they held the wedding on an auspicious day and gave the flower-garlanded maiden to the young man, so it is told.
1490.event: Kemasari is married to Civakan on an auspicious day amid the city's music.

1491.reading: Such was the joy of the man with shoulders like gem-pots pressed close, who never let go of the woman whose beauty no astrologer could measure.

1492.reading: Her silk-clad breasts became the mountain, his twin shoulders the serpent, and the sea of her compassion, churned, gave him nectar, as they say.
1492.nuance: The union is told as the churning of the ocean: she is mountain and sea, he the cord-serpent, and the nectar is what she gives; the borrowed myth makes the pleasure divine in kind.

1493.reading: As the bangled girl's breasts plunged into the sandal mire and she leapt to him, the youth's garland was crushed and her anklets and girdle cried out with open mouths.

1494.reading: Garlands and hair tumbling, pearls of the ornaments sinking as they struck, their love and delight swelling, they did not part night or day and were like those who have won the state with neither death nor birth.
1494.event: Civakan and Kemasari stay together without parting, night and day.
1494.nuance: சாதலும் பிறப்பும் இல்லாத் தன்மை is the language of release from rebirth, and the narrator gives it to two lovers in bed; it is a simile (ஒத்தார்), not a claim that pleasure frees, and the same night of 1504 ends it.

1495.reading: The garlanded man and the woman like a flowering branch went through budding groves and cool clear streams, plucked lilies from the springs and crowned each other, enjoying the good of their deeds, people made eminent by fate.
1495.event: The couple wander the pleasure groves and pools together.

claims.claim: the pleasures one enjoys are the fruit of one's good deeds, given by fate

1495.nuance: வினைநலம் நுகர்ந்து and விதியினான் put the honeymoon in the book of karma: their delight is not earned in this life but eaten as the ripened good of earlier deeds.

1496.reading: As their overflowing love went on with no loosening of embrace, two months passed, and one day the youth went with the woman of pressed-out femininity into a grove of chosen flowers on a hill of falling cascades.
1496.event: After two months of marriage, Civakan takes Kemasari to a flower grove on a hill with waterfalls.

1497.reading: He climbed with splendour the hill of sweet springs and falls, ringed by golden areca, plantains with ripe clusters, flowering naga trees and camphor groves, where peacocks dance on mango boughs and champak drops its flowers.

1498.reading: On the millet slope the little red-beaked parrots, taking the bangled woman's voice for a parrot's, would not fly off; ashamed, she waved her golden garland, and the hero with ringing anklets came near and drove the parrots away himself.
1498.event: Kemasari tries to scare the parrots from the millet; they take her voice for their own, and Civakan drives them off.
1498.nuance: The scene is the akam scene of the girl guarding the millet field (தினை, கிளி ஓப்புதல்) moved into marriage; the joke that her voice is too parrot-like to frighten parrots makes her embarrassment (நாணி) the point.

1499.reading: He praised her: creeper who ate up my life with your spear-like eyes, I have come bearing a garland of red leaves to worship your small feet; shall I live on and serve you, or leave this body and go? Doll, command me.
1499.event: Civakan offers Kemasari a leaf garland and asks her to command him.
1499.nuance: The choice he puts to her, to live and serve or to leave the body and go (உடம்பு ஒழித்து ஏகுவேனோ), is a lover's hyperbole, but its verb of going returns as the plain event of 1505, when he leaves her without asking.

1500.reading: Saying that merchants' daughters are the ones truly skilled in trade, since her parrot-sweet lisping speech outsold vina, flute, milk, nectar, sugarcane, honey and the music of the lute, he embraced her till her ornamented breasts swelled and drank her beauty.
1500.event: Civakan praises Kemasari's speech and embraces her.
1500.nuance: The pun on வாணிகம் plays on her birth: a merchant's daughter who has 'sold' him sweetness outbidding every sweet thing; it is also the second time in the chapter (after விற்குமே in 1485) that her worth is put as a price.

1501.reading: As the young moon glimmers against the red sky, so she lay on his saffron chest; sitting with her, the man of fragrant garland, minded to leave in the night, saw a gem-bee at the lily of her bright wide eye and spoke.
1501.event: Civakan, sitting with Kemasari, sees a bee near her eye and speaks to it.
1501.nuance: கங்குல் தான் நீங்கல் உற்று is read here as his intent to leave by night, which makes the bee-speech that follows a covert farewell; it may instead mean only that night was passing.

1502.reading: He tells the gem-bee that when it came to drink honey from this lady's garland, its mate, left behind, would sit grieving without song, and that if its mate sleeps it too will sleep; so its partner stays on with tender grief.
1502.nuance: Spoken to a bee in her presence, the verse seems to rehearse his own leaving: the one who goes for honey and the mate who stays behind grieving. The second half is hard to construe, and the sense of பணிகொண்டது இன்மை is not fixed.

1503.reading: The sun, born an infant, grown a young man and then a desireless old man whose bright rays fade, fell; and he crowned the parrot-voiced woman with a jasmine garland where lisping bees wandered and went with her to the couch fragrant with smoke.
1503.event: At sunset Civakan garlands Kemasari and goes to bed with her.
1503.nuance: The sunset is told as a whole human life in a day (குழவி, குமரன், கிழவன்), and விழைவுதீர் gives the old sun the very loss of desire that the lovers do not yet feel; the image of impermanence frames the last night before he leaves.

1504.reading: When the woman, wearied by the toil of pleasure after his garland had crushed her, closed her sword-bright lily eyes, he rose, turned from the golden one and went to the many-gemmed door with its strong coral bolt.
1504.event: While Kemasari sleeps, Civakan rises and goes to the door.
1504.nuance: புறக்கணித்து, 'turning his back on', is a strong verb for a hero leaving a bride of two months; the verse gives no reason for the going.

1505.reading: Pressing the door softly so that the lady like the doll in the lotus should not know, he opened it, and the man like a lion of killing rage crossed the treasure-filled mansion and went into the spreading dark like the many-rayed sun.
1505.event: Civakan opens the door secretly and leaves Kemasari's house in the dark.
1505.nuance: The simile of the sun going into darkness reverses the sun of 1503, which fell; here the hero is the light that leaves and the house is left dark. The secrecy (அறிவுறா வகையின்) is the centre of the verse.

1506.reading: The lotus-faced woman with bright ornaments, who had rested on his chest, does not see even in dream the husband whose love grew daily like the laughing moon.
1506.nuance: கனவிற் காணாள: she does not see him even in dream, so the dream that in akam poetry consoles the separated woman is denied her; her sleep is unbroken while he goes.

1507.reading: When he had slipped away as night ended, she of gold-sprouting breasts, like a boon-giving goddess, woke from her heavy sleep, looked in every direction, and slowly grew distressed.
1507.event: Kemasari wakes, finds Civakan gone, and searches with her eyes.

1508.reading: Unable to find the man like the dark pupil of an eye where he had hidden, the woman like a flowering golden branch ran through the lamp-lit mansion until the dark lifted, like a serpent that has lost its rare gem.
1508.event: Kemasari runs through the mansion searching for Civakan.
1508.nuance: Two images of loss meet: he is கருமணிப் பாவை, the pupil of her eye, so his going leaves her blind; and she is the serpent without its gem, a creature that in lore cannot see or live without the jewel it carries.

links.note: The Kural's man asks whether Vishnu's world is sweeter than sleep in the beloved's arms; the epic answers by likening the lovers to those beyond birth and death.
links.teaches: Set beside the Kural's open question, the Jain epic lends sexual bliss the very vocabulary of release, then ends that bliss within the chapter by the hero's leaving.

gains.a: the epic's simile is shown to answer a known question about whether love can rival the gods' world
gains.b: the couplet's question receives a narrative test, in which the answer 'yes' holds only for two months

links.note: The Kural's lover says the beloved is life when present and death when she leaves; Civakan offers to live serving her or leave his body, then is himself the one who leaves.
links.teaches: The couplet assumes the woman is the one who departs and the man the one who dies of it; the epic reverses the roles, so the parting the man dreads is the parting he chooses.

gains.a: Civakan's live-or-die hyperbole is shown to be a formula of the lover's art, not a vow
gains.b: the couplet's life-and-death image is seen from the side of the one who goes rather than the one left

links.note: Civakan asks her to command whether he lives to serve her or goes; six verses on he goes without a word to her.
links.teaches: The hero's offer to let her decide his going is contradicted by a departure she is not even awake to know of.

links.note: Naladiyar makes the sun Death's daily measure of one's days; the epic tells one day's sun as a whole life from infant to desireless old man, and the lovers go to bed.
links.teaches: The epic uses the Naladiyar's moral image of the sun as a life measured out, but withholds its moral, letting the lovers' indifference to the dying sun foreshadow the night that ends their union.

gains.a: the sunset's life-stages carry the ethical charge of the day as a portion of life eaten by Death
gains.b: the quatrain's abstract measure gains a concrete picture of a day as infancy, youth and old age

links.note: The patikam sums up the Takka episode as living with the merchant's daughter as one life and then leaving her; here the leaving is told.
links.teaches: The patikam's bare 'he left her' becomes a stealthy departure from a sleeping bride, so the summary's single verb hides the secrecy the story stresses.

links.note: The Kural's woman demands to be told whether her man will go; Civakan leaves while Kemasari sleeps, so that she cannot ask.
links.teaches: The secret night departure is the hero's way of avoiding exactly the plea the couplet voices, and the couplet names what Kemasari is denied: the chance to speak before the going.

gains.a: Kemasari's silent loss is given the words she never gets to say
gains.b: the couplet's plea is shown its counter-move, a leaving timed so the plea cannot be made

links.note: Here the lovers' delight is called the eating of the good of their deeds; in 408 the teacher leaves to do penance that wears away old deeds.
links.teaches: Within one Jain epic, pleasure counted as the good fruit of deeds is still deeds, the very store that the renouncer's penance sets out to wear away.

source_issues: 1487: printed in 5 lines; lines 2 and 3 (ஊன்கறி கற்ற கால / னொண்மணித் தடக்கை வைவேல்) are one line of the stanza broken in two.
1500 line 1: வீணையுஞ் குழலும் has a nasal (ஞ்) that does not agree with the following க; the expected form is வீணையுங் குழலும், likely a typographical slip.
1501-1504 and 1506-1508: printed in 8 half-lines and joined into 4 by the build; the joins read correctly.
1502: the second half (துணைவண்டு துஞ்சின் நீயும் துஞ்சுவை ... பணிகொண்டது இன்மையால்) is hard to construe and may be corrupt.
